newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW- Ramco sees Azeri progress, some hurdles.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW- Ramco sees Azeri progress, some hurdles.

text.p: British independent oil services and exploration company Ramco Energy Plc says it is making progress with plans to develop a massive onshore field in Azerbaijan but obstacles remain.

Ramco has signed a preliminary agreement on commercial terms covering a joint venture with the State Oil Company of the Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR) to develop the Muradhanli field -- estimated to have one billion barrels of low sulphur crude reserves -- but taxation matters were still being discussed. "We have signed off on the preliminary terms that would govern the joint venture economics, but it's now really the outstanding fiscal terms that have to be resolved," chairman Stephen Remp told Reuters.

Remp said several key questions concerning joint venture taxation needed to be clarified with the Azeri government and terms would have to be improved before Western companies would invest in tapping the country's huge onshore potential.
"It's now a government decision. To date there has been no serious Western interest in onshore Azerbaijan," Remp said in an interview.
"Ramco is really leading the charge in terms of trying to ensure the Azeris act in their own best interest."

The current taxation regime made onshore projects uneconomic and was deterring pent-up interest from Western oil majors, independents and service companies encouraged by the performance of an international consortium which is developing three giant offshore fields in the Caspian.

The 12-company Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC) has agreements with Russia and Georgia to transport early production, starting at 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) in a year's time via two separate pipelines to the Black Sea. Ramco has a 2.1 percent stake in the AIOC.
"The Azeris need to provide at least the same incentives as have been given to offshore projects," Remp said.
Earlier this summer, Ramco signed an alliance agreement with Schlumberger Logelco Inc, which will act as field management contractor in the development of Muradhanli.
Schlumberger will drill two or three wells to determine the commercial viability of the field.

Meanwhile, Ramco continues to look for other opportunities in the former Soviet Union, devoting particular attention to Kazakhstan and Georgia. "I have been cautious about Kazakhstan for a long time but now it is beginning to look attractive," said Remp, citing Chevron Corp's Tengiz field in the northwest of the country and the possibility of a dedicated export route as positive factors.
"We are also casting one eye over Ukraine and two eyes over Georgia," he added.
Russia, the world's third largest oil producer, remains a long-term possibility but is well down Ramco's priority list.

"Russia continues to disappoint every Western oil investor I know...In my view the Russians are still not convinced about the value of Western investment -- they want the money but not the companies," Remp said.
"We are reducing our focus on Russia, waiting for better times to appear."
